sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
The common-gate stage is fast because its gate sits at AC ground. No capacitor connects its input to its output, so nothing is Miller-multiplied. Each capacitance simply loads one node to ground, and each node gives its own pole.

At the **input**, the source node sees the driver's resistance \(R_s\) in parallel with the device's own \(1/g_m\), which is usually small. Its capacitance, mainly \(C_{gs}\) plus \(C_{sb}\), therefore gives a high-frequency pole, often near the device's \(f_T\). At the **output**, the drain node sees the full load resistance \(R_L\) with \(C_{gd}\), \(C_{db}\) and any load capacitance. That pole is usually dominant. With two well-separated, non-interacting poles, the bandwidth is essentially the output pole. The analysis is clean only while \(r_o\) is large. A finite \(r_o\) couples the two nodes, because the CG input resistance then depends on the load.

The gate is grounded, so no capacitor bridges input and output.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: A CG stage with \(g_m = 5\ \mathrm{mS}\), \(R_s = 300\ \Omega\) and \(C_{gs} = 25\ \mathrm{fF}\) has an input pole at \(1/[2\pi(300\parallel200)(25\ \mathrm{fF})] = 53\ \mathrm{GHz}\). Its 6 kΩ drain with 30 fF has an output pole at 884 MHz, which sets the bandwidth.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Multiplying \(C_{gd}\) by the gain; it goes straight to AC ground here.
- Using \(R_s\) alone for the input node and forgetting \(1/g_m\).
- Assuming the input pole dominates.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Stacking a CG device on a CS device gives the cascode, whose internal node inherits this low-resistance, high-frequency pole.
